title: Impact of extraction methods on the properties of Carica papaya pseudostem fibers from Cameroon used as reinforcement in

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ("In contrast to the decrease in diameter...") vs. Section 3.1.2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states that diameter decreased while density increased with NaOH concentration, implying a monotonic decrease with alkali concentration. The results give 302.02 µm (water), 196.33 µm (2.5 % NaOH), 221.94 µm (5 % NaOH) and 219.31 µm (7.5 % NaOH): diameter reaches a minimum at 2.5 % and then increases again, so no monotonic 'decrease in diameter' with NaOH exists.

"This indicates that the NaOH extraction process creates a narrowing of diameters due to the removal of non-cellulosic material" is not supported by the reported values, where 5 % and 7.5 % NaOH give larger diameters (221.94 and 219.31 µm) than 2.5 % (196.33 µm). The data cannot establish a dose-dependent narrowing effect.

Yield (dried fibre mass / initial mass, Eq. 1) is reported to INCREASE with NaOH concentration (17.98 → 19.92 → 24.39 → 28.63 %), and this is attributed to "the effectiveness of NaOH in eliminating non-cellulosic elements and thus favoring fiber recovery". Removing non-cellulosic material (hemicellulose, lignin, pectin, waxes) necessarily removes mass and should lower, not raise, the mass-based yield; the stated mechanism contradicts the trend it is used to explain.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.2 vs. Section 2.3 / Section 2.3 yield determination
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 2.2 states the water-retted fibres were "rinsed and sun-dried for 24 h to remove moisture", while Section 2.3 states that "the fibers extracted by the different techniques were dried at 28 °C in the sun for 72 h" and the yield (Eq. 1) is computed from "dried masses of the fibers after drying for 72 h". The drying protocol for the water-retted fibres is therefore inconsistent, which directly affects the reported yield comparison.

predicted_errors.error_location: Sections 2.5.1 (FTIR) and 2.5.2 (TGA) – "powder (0.3 μm)" / "ground to a size of 0.3 μm"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Grinding lignocellulosic fibres to a sub-micron (0.3 µm) particle size is not achievable with conventional laboratory grinding and is inconsistent with the ~20 mg sample preparation described; the stated particle size is almost certainly wrong by three orders of magnitude (0.3 mm) and makes the described procedure impossible as written.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.5 (pycnometric density, Eq. 3) and abstract density range
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Absolute density is measured by water pycnometry with the sample immersed in demineralised water for 24 h, yet the same fibres are reported to absorb 141–159 % of their mass in water in 24 h. Water uptake and swelling invalidate the displacement measurement, and the resulting value of 0.633 g cm⁻³ for water-retted fibre (far below the 0.943 and 1.12 g cm⁻³ reported for Indian and Brazilian papaya fibres in the introduction) is physically implausible for a water-saturated lignocellulosic fibre.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction – "Cameroon ranks 64th in the world in papaya production, with an annual output of 44 tons"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: An annual national output of only 44 tonnes is incompatible with a 64th world ranking (countries at that rank produce tens of thousands of tonnes) and with the stated premise that papaya pseudostems are "widely available as biomass waste". The figure is off by several orders of magnitude (likely thousands of tonnes).

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction – "dominated by three fibers (flax, hemp, and coir) that alone account for over 80 % of production, excluding cotton [10]"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: World non-cotton natural fibre production is dominated by jute (and jute-like fibres), which alone exceeds flax, hemp and coir combined; the claim as attributed to ref. [10] misrepresents natural-fibre production statistics.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1.2 – "likely to make them denser, less hydrophilic due to their porous nature"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The statement is self-contradictory: increased porosity would raise, not lower, water uptake, and 'denser' is incompatible with 'porous'. The explanation offered for the reduced absorption contradicts basic physics of the proposed mechanism.

The text states "Traditionally, lignocellulosic and bast fibers were extracted by the dew retting process. Dew retting is also an alternative and sustainable method... However, due to the longer lead times and water pollution problems associated with water retting..." The passage confuses dew retting with water retting (repeats dew retting as both traditional and the alternative, then attributes drawbacks to water retting), making the stated justification for alternative extraction methods incoherent.

A drop from 220 °C (water retting) to 215 °C (2.5 % NaOH) is described as part of a "clear decrease"; a 5 °C difference, with no uncertainty reported for TGA onset temperatures, does not support the stated conclusion for the 2.5 % condition.

Strain is defined as ε = Δl/l (a dimensionless ratio) but results are reported in percent (3.505 ± 1.01 %); the factor of 100 is missing from the equation as written. Likewise the tensile modulus (8.271 ± 1.62) is reported without units in the abstract.
